published_statement: Sec. IX: 'The same cautionary note applies to the main theorems of this paper which, following on the earlier work of Geroch and Tipler, appear to forbid topology change. Their true value is not so much that they actually rule out topology change, but rather that they allow us to pinpoint what modifications we have to make in our general framework so as to allow it. A popular modification (for a number of reasons, not all directly related to the specific problem of topology change) is to abandon the Lorentzian framework altogether and to use a Euclidean path integral formalism. But even within the general Lorentzian framework there are still several interesting possibilities.' A] Dropping causal compactness: 'it is hard to see that it could be replaced by a weaker assumption that still restricts the candidates ... without some restriction ... these manifolds can be cut and truncated in an entirely arbitrary manner. Also, there is the theorem of Tipler (ref. [8], Theorem 5) ... (in the closed universe case) that if topology change occurs via a non-compact interpolating spacetime, then it contains (under some mild additional assumptions) a singularity (in the sense of an incomplete timelike geodesic) or a point at infinity. That it is a singularity that must occur may be inferred only under the significant additional assumption that there is an upper bound on the lengths of certain timelike curves ... the presence of points at infinity is still a highly undesirable feature.' B] Weakening the curvature constraints: 'This would not affect the presence of causality violations, but it might permit topology change as a dynamical process. A drastic step in this direction would be to alter Einstein's equation ... But such an alteration would have to be fairly severe ... Another possibility is ... that there might be violations of the energy conditions large enough to allow assumption (ii) to be violated. Some discussions of wormhole creation are, for example, based precisely on large violations of the energy condition.' C] Degenerate metrics: 'it might be possible to allow the metric to vanish or to become degenerate at isolated points and to use these kinds of singularities in order to get topology change ... even in standard general relativity (couched in first-order language) Horowitz [20] has shown that it is possible to construct reasonable topology-changing spacetimes if degenerate metrics are allowed. So, this might well prove to be the correct approach to describing topology change.' Followed by: 'the causal structure that is normally associated with a Lorentz metric will not necessarily be well-defined. But there is a way around this ...' Sec. VIII: 'If we were satisfied with metrics that are only continuous ... S1 and S2 need not be diffeomorphic, even if causality violations are forbidden.'
published_hypotheses: The list is Borde's own and is framed as non-exhaustive: 'several interesting possibilities' within the Lorentzian framework, plus the Euclidean route outside it. It is offered as modifications that 'allow' topology change, not as a proof that every way out fails.

The escapes are relative to the paper's framework: a smooth, non-degenerate, time-oriented Lorentz metric on a causally compact interpolating manifold (Theorems 1 and 3). 'All of these comments are valid only under the assumptions of this paper ... it is always possible that different conclusions may be drawn if different assumptions are made.'

A] relies on Tipler's Theorem 5, which holds in the closed-universe case, for a non-compact interpolant, 'under some mild additional assumptions'. It yields a singularity OR a point at infinity. A singularity specifically needs 'the significant additional assumption' of an upper bound on timelike lengths. Yodzis: a conformal rescaling can push the singularity to infinity.

B] keeps causal compactness, so Theorem 1's causality violation stays ('would not affect the presence of causality violations'). B has two sub-routes: (1) alter Einstein's equation ('fairly severe'; 'no real justification -- theoretical or experimental'); (2) keep Einstein's equation and violate the energy conditions enough to break Theorem 3's assumption (ii).

C] lets the metric vanish or degenerate at isolated points. Borde calls these 'these kinds of singularities'. He places C 'within the general Lorentzian framework', notes Horowitz does it 'even in standard general relativity (couched in first-order language)', and says the usual causal structure 'will not necessarily be well-defined'.
'Singularity' means the standard incomplete-geodesic definition. Other definitions can change the misconception verdicts.
Sec. VIII (outside the IX list): with C^0 metrics the diffeomorphism conclusion fails even without causality violation.

later_literature.ref: arXiv:2202.09833v4 (Garcia-Heveling 2022/2024), 'Topology change with Morse functions: progress on the Borde-Sorkin conjecture'
later_literature.what: Develops route C], the route the tree omits. With metrics that degenerate at isolated Morse points, topology change can occur without CTCs ('the only way to have topology change without time travel is by allowing the spacetime metric to degenerate'). It proves a special case of the Borde-Sorkin conjecture, argues the original conjecture is false, and proposes a refined form. It notes non-compact slices allow topology change without CTCs or singular points (Sanchez, NAMED-NOT-READ). That matches the tree's H_closed scoping of route A. As recorded by the earlier audit, it treats the degenerate points as places where 'nothing special happens'. That is the reading under which z3 E10 has the tree's claim FAIL.

later_literature.ref: arXiv:gr-qc/9711070 (Dowker & Surya 1998), 'Topology Change and Causal Continuity'
later_literature.what: With Morse (degenerate) metrics, 'no topological cobordism is excluded'. In 3+1 dimensions, if the Borde-Sorkin conjecture holds, every transition can be done by a causally continuous cobordism with only index-2 points. The S^3 -> S^2 x S^1 wormhole transition has an index-2 route. This makes route C] a live candidate for exactly the tree's case, conditional on a conjecture.

lacked_data: M's hypothesis tested for this result. Borde's escape list uses no measured datum, so no later measurement can move it (data_at_publication). What Borde lacked in 1994 was mathematics, not data: the causal theory of degenerate (Morse) metrics that his C] points to ('This will be discussed in detail elsewhere [57]'). That theory came later (Borde-Dowker-Garcia-Sorkin-Surya 1999, NAMED-NOT-READ; Dowker-Surya 1998; Garcia-Heveling 2022-24, read earlier this session). It strengthens C] as a route to topology change without CTCs, at the price of isolated metric degeneracies, and in 3+1 it rests on a conjecture now refined. Explicit non-degenerate nucleations (2505.02210) confirm the other side: when the metric is kept non-degenerate, the CTC price is paid. So the evidence on M's hypothesis runs both ways. Borde's own statements stand and nothing he wrote is refuted. The incompleteness is in the tree's use, which lists three of Borde's four routes, drops the one Borde thought might be 'the correct approach', and declares by hand that none stays in GR. Whether a degenerate point is a 'pathology' is a definitional ruling this audit does not make: Borde calls such points 'these kinds of singularities', and later authors treat them as benign. The later work shows that the route is live. It does not show that it escapes in the tree's sense.
grade_evidence: What Borde wrote is quoted correctly. Every fragment is verbatim (E2), and the three routes the tree lists carry the outcomes Borde gives them under the closed-universe case (E10: FOLLOWS). No datum enters. The tree's USE rests on a smaller class than the source, in ways shown here. (1) 'ALL THREE' adds an exhaustiveness Borde does not claim ('several interesting possibilities') and drops his route C], degenerate metrics, which he places within the Lorentzian framework and calls possibly 'the correct approach' (E3, E4). With C] (or the Sec. VIII C^0 route) included, z3 finds the tree's 'none stays in Lorentzian GR without a pathology' UNDETERMINED, and its truth turns on whether a degenerate point counts as a pathology. (2) create.py omits A]'s closed-universe case and Tipler's additional assumptions (E6). Without them the claim is UNDETERMINED (z3). specthm restores them as H_closed, so the gated fact is correctly scoped while create.py's sentence is not. (3) B] is recorded without its energy-condition sub-route and without 'would not affect the presence of causality violations' (E5). That omission does not change the verdict (z3 FOLLOWS with it added), but it misreports the source. (4) The in-GR flags are hand-set literals (E9): READ for the three listed, not computed. (5) The 'VIII.A' citation should be IX.A, a discrepancy and not an error. Not WRONG: nothing Borde states is contradicted. The tree's claim is true for the routes it lists under H_closed, and no counterexample to it is shown here, only an undetermined case. Not DATA-DEPENDENT: no datum. Not STANDS: an added exhaustiveness hypothesis and a dropped route are NARROWED's definition.
what_would_change_the_grade: To STANDS: the tree (a) lists C] (degenerate metrics) and B's energy-condition sub-route among Borde's routes, (b) marks C]'s in-GR flag OPEN, or rules explicitly (a ruling for M) that an isolated metric degeneracy is a pathology or a departure from GR under M-S1A-P3, in which case z3 returns FOLLOWS, (c) states the closed-universe case in create.py's section 4, and (d) corrects VIII.A to IX.A. To WRONG for the tree's use: a ruling or demonstration, inside the tree's own definitions, that a degenerate-metric (or C^0) topology change stays in Lorentzian GR without a pathology. z3 shows the claim then FAILS. That needs a definitional ruling, not a computation this audit can make. For Borde himself: nothing, since the section proves nothing and claims only possibilities.
